channel.title: MEV-X Blog
channel.description: Research and engineering notes on MEV protection, atomic arbitrage, AMM yield, and DEX infrastructure from the team behind MEV-X.

item.title: Every Chain Handles MEV Differently — One Decided to Keep It Inside
item.description: Ethereum's PBS, Solana's Jito marketplace, and Sui's object model each treat MEV differently. A comparison of chain-level MEV protection models, and what changes when a protocol captures value directly.

item.title: Homelander Security Audit by Bailsec: Algebra Plugin
item.description: A differential audit of Homelander's Algebra plugin update — and why extending an already-audited execution model carries a different risk profile than shipping a new one.

item.title: QuickSwap Integrates Homelander: MEV Internalization as a DEX Standard
item.description: QuickSwap's community vote to integrate Homelander passed 3.2M QUICK in favor, zero against. What that says about where DEX infrastructure and AMM yield are heading.

item.title: Homelander Security Audit: Uniswap v4 — Summary and Outcomes
item.description: MixBytes' audit of Homelander's Uniswap v4 hook implementation found no critical or high-severity issues, confirming the hook contains external-execution failures without touching the user's swap.

item.title: Homelander Is Expanding to Uniswap v4
item.description: With Uniswap Foundation grant support, Homelander moves onto v4's hook architecture — and the afterSwap hook becomes the atomic MEV capture point.

item.title: Where MEV Actually Comes From
item.description: Four independent attribution methods trace 96.7% of atomic arbitrage on Polygon back to a single source transaction. What that means for how MEV protection should be designed.

item.title: MEV Internalization: Keeping Value Inside the Protocol
item.description: A protocol has three options for the MEV its own activity creates: ignore it, capture it natively, or route it to a partner. MEV leakage isn't actually unavoidable.

item.title: Homelander Security Audit: Summary and Outcomes
item.description: Bailsec's first security audit of Homelander found no exploitable vulnerabilities — and confirmed that a failed internal MEV path can never touch the user's swap outcome.

item.title: MEV Resolution in AMM-Based Systems: External vs Internal
item.description: Every swap that moves an AMM pool off market price creates an arbitrage opportunity. Who closes it — an external searcher or the protocol itself — decides who keeps the value.

item.title: Introducing Homelander: Atomic MEV Internalization
item.description: Homelander captures post-swap arbitrage atomically, in the same transaction as the swap that created it — turning MEV that would leak to external searchers into AMM yield.
